newsitem.title: ISRAEL: BZW says Israel Fund winding-up due to discount.
newsitem.headline: BZW says Israel Fund winding-up due to discount.

text.p: BZW said on Thursday that a proposal to liquidate its $150 million Israel Fund does not reflect negative sentiment on the part of foreign investors towards the Israeli market.

The board of the Israel Fund, one of the largest foreign investors in the Tel Aviv market, announced on Tuesday that after discussions with major shareholders it would propose undertaking "an orderly realisation of the assets of the company (fund) followed by the winding up of the company".
"It has nothing to do with Israel. The fund could be trading in Brazil, Poland or Mars," fund manager Lysander Tennant told Reuters.
Israel Fund Plc had said in August it was reviewing options for enhancing shareholder value and Baring Brothers was brought in to act as financial advisers.

"The fund's performance has been quite satisfactory in the recent period and the Israeli market has performed as well, despite everything else that is going on," said a director at Barings who asked not to be named.
After a three-year slump, the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange's Mishtanim index rose 40 percent from November to a record high in mid-February. It has since fallen back 11.5 percent.
The decision to liquidate the fund is a result of pressure from shareholders who were dissatisfied with the fund's discount.
"The board has been trying to deal with the discount," Tennant said.

The closed-end fund is currently trading at an 8.5 to 9.0 percent discount to net asset value, which industry sources said is typical for a country fund. But the discount was as wide as 20 percent before news that a restructuring was in the works.
Tennant said the board's recommendation to distribute the assets would likely be passed by shareholders.
"It is very sad, not at all what we would have liked," he said.
Another fund investing in Israeli shares -- U.S. based Israel Growth Fund -- closed in January after failing to raise enough money due to the crisis in the Middle East peace process.
That fund was launched a year ago, just after a wave of suicide bombings in Israel killed 59 people. It managed to raise only $11.5 million in nine months.

More recent discouragement has come from the start of work on a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem which has ignited violence, including the killing of three Israeli women last week by a Palestinian who blew himself up at a Tel Aviv cafe.
But Tennant said the Israel Fund's investors were not shaken by heightened tension between Israelis and Palestinians nor by the market's recent weakness.
He noted that major shareholders, representing 43.3 percent of the company's issued shares, have expressed support for an in-specie option which offers shares held by the fund rather than cash.
BZW will continue to invest in Israeli shares through its general emerging market fund, Tennant said.
